# The Sieve

In April of 1229, a scribe named Johannes Myronas finished making a prayer book in Jerusalem. He signed it, dated it, and asked whoever used it to pray for him. To make it, he had taken apart several older books, washed their leaves with milk and lye, scraped them with pumice, cut each leaf in half, and rotated the halves ninety degrees so the old writing ran sideways beneath the new. One of the books he dismantled had been copied in Constantinople some two hundred and fifty years earlier. It contained the only surviving copy of a work by Archimedes called *The Method of Mechanical Theorems*, in which Archimedes explains not how he proved his results but how he *found* them — and in which he does something no one else would do for eighteen centuries, which is to treat an infinite collection of lines as a quantity you can compare in size to another infinite collection of lines.

Myronas did not know this. Or if he suspected there was geometry under the liturgy, he did not think it outweighed the liturgy. He was not a vandal. He was a man with a deadline and a finite supply of goatskin.

I keep returning to that — not the tragedy of it but the ordinariness. We tell the loss of ancient knowledge as a story of fires: Alexandria burning, barbarians at the gates, monks in a dark age. It makes for a satisfying narrative because it has villains and a moment. But the fire story is mostly wrong, and the truth is much stranger and, I think, much more unsettling. Almost nothing was destroyed. Almost everything simply stopped being copied.

---

Consider what it actually took for a text to reach us. Every book in the ancient world existed only as a set of physical objects, and every physical object decays. Papyrus in a damp climate lasts a century or two at best. Parchment does better but not indefinitely. So a text survived only if, roughly every couple of hundred years, somebody found it worth the enormous labor of reproducing by hand. A long work might take a scribe months. Multiply that across twenty-two centuries and you have a relay race with somewhere between ten and thirty legs, no finish line, and a rule that if any single runner drops the baton, the race is over forever.

Now ask what the odds are. Ask it about a specific play by Sophocles. It has to be copied in Alexandria in the third century BCE, and in Rome or Antioch in the second century CE, and in Constantinople in the fifth, and again in the ninth, and again in the twelfth, and it has to be in a library that gets catalogued rather than one that gets damp, and it has to survive the specific week when some specific person decides the shelf space is needed for something else. Every one of those is a coin flip weighted against it. The miracle is not that we lost most of Greek literature. The miracle is that we have any of it at all.

We have seven plays by Sophocles out of something like a hundred and twenty. Seven by Aeschylus out of seventy or ninety. Eighteen by Euripides out of ninety. Livy wrote a hundred and forty-two books of Roman history; thirty-five come down to us. Polybius wrote forty; five are complete. Aristotle's published dialogues — the ones Cicero praised as a flowing river of gold — are gone entirely.

That last one deserves a pause, because it scrambles something most people carry around unexamined. We think of Aristotle as dry. Systematic, taxonomic, difficult, a man who writes like a filing cabinet. That impression is entirely an artifact of transmission. What survived is his *esoteric* corpus: lecture notes, research materials, the working documents of a research institute. The polished prose he actually released to the public, the stuff that made him famous as a stylist, evaporated. We have the syllabus and not the performance, and we have mistaken the syllabus for the man.

The Stoics are worse. Chrysippus, the third head of the Stoa, reportedly wrote over seven hundred books and was considered so essential that people said if there were no Chrysippus there would be no Stoa. Essentially nothing survives. We know his arguments mainly through quotations in the works of people attacking him. What we *do* have of Stoicism is a Roman politician's moral letters, a freedman's lecture notes taken down by a student, and a Roman emperor's private journal. The system-builders are gone and the self-help survived. So when someone today says "the Stoics believed," they are usually describing a tradition whose entire technical architecture has been deleted and whose remaining surface happens to be the part that reads well on a phone at six in the morning.

---

Why did those particular things make it through? Two great bottlenecks, and both of them were technological.

The first was the shift from the scroll to the codex — the bound book with pages — which happened across roughly the second to fourth centuries CE. Codices won decisively: you can write on both sides, you can flip to a passage instead of unrolling twenty feet, you can shelve them upright, you can fit four gospels in one object. But during the transition, a text had to be *transferred*. Somebody had to decide it was worth recopying into the new format. Anything not transferred became a scroll in a world of codices, and scrolls in that world were, functionally, trash.

The second bottleneck was subtler and probably deadlier. In the ninth century, Byzantine scribes adopted minuscule — a compact, cursive, ligatured script that was faster to write and fit far more text on a page. The old majuscule hands, all capitals, became obsolete. Once again, a text had to be *transliterated* to stay alive. If nobody transliterated it, it sat on a shelf in a script that fewer and fewer people could comfortably read, in a format nobody was producing anymore, until it quietly rotted.

The vast majority of what we lost, we lost at that second gate. Not to fire. To a font change.

And what got transliterated? Whatever was useful. School texts, above all — the small set of authors that the Byzantine curriculum drilled into boys. Grammar, rhetoric, medicine, law, mathematics that someone still needed, and Christian writers, who had an institutional apparatus devoted to their reproduction that no pagan author could match. Selection pressure ran toward the teachable and the practical. The odd, the difficult, the specialized, the enormous, and the unfashionable were left in capitals.

Here is the detail that made me want to write this at all. The seven Sophocles plays we have are not a random sample and not a greatest-hits collection chosen by posterity. They are a *school anthology*. Somebody in late antiquity selected seven plays for classroom use, annotated them, and that annotated selection got copied because teachers needed it. The other hundred and thirteen had no institutional constituency and died.

Euripides is the exception that proves the mechanism. We have eighteen of his plays rather than seven, and the extra eleven exist because of an accident: a single volume of an alphabetical collected edition — the plays whose Greek titles began with the letters epsilon through kappa — happened to survive without commentary, outside the school selection. *Helen*, *Electra*, *Ion*, *Iphigenia among the Taurians*, *Heracles*. Those are among his strangest and best works, and they came through not because anyone judged them excellent but because a chunk of an alphabet got lucky.

So the shape of the Greek canon is: a late-antique syllabus, plus one alphabetical accident.

---

The accidents elsewhere are almost unbearable to think about.

Menander was the most admired comic playwright of the Hellenistic world and for two thousand years existed only as quotations — a line here, a maxim there, preserved because someone liked the phrasing. Then papyri started coming out of Egypt. Some of it came from ancient garbage dumps. Some of it came from crocodile mummies: at Tebtunis, embalmers stuffed the sacred crocodiles with wastepaper, and the wastepaper was discarded books. In 1907 a nearly complete Menander play turned up in a codex from Cairo. *Dyskolos*, the Grouch, essentially intact, not published until 1958. We recovered a masterpiece from a reptile's padding.

Cicero's *De re publica* survived because someone scraped it off and wrote Augustine's commentary on the Psalms over it. Angelo Mai found it in the Vatican in 1819 and recognized the ghost underneath. The most influential Roman political treatise exists in fragments because a monk needed the pages, and we have even those fragments because Augustine was popular enough that *his* text got preserved, dragging Cicero along beneath it like a body under ice.

And at Herculaneum, in a villa buried by Vesuvius, there are roughly eighteen hundred scrolls that were carbonized rather than burned — turned into charcoal cylinders that look like burnt logs and fall apart if you touch them. For two hundred and fifty years, opening them meant destroying them. Now they can be scanned and the ink distinguished from the substrate computationally, because the ink sits slightly proud of the surface. In late 2023 a student reading a scan found the word *porphyras*. Purple. Then more, then columns of it, a passage about pleasure and music and food, probably Epicurean, possibly Philodemus. It is the first new classical text in generations that nobody had to dig up. It came out of a machine looking at a shape.

---

What I find hardest is not the loss but the *shape* of the loss — that absence has no texture.

If a library burns, you can at least sometimes reconstruct the catalogue. Callimachus made one for Alexandria: the *Pinakes*, a hundred and twenty scrolls listing authors and their works, the first serious bibliography. It is also lost. We have the table of contents of a library we do not have, and only in pieces, quoted by others.

Most of the time we do not even get that. We do not know what the missing hundred and thirteen Sophocles plays were about. We cannot miss them specifically. They do not exert pressure on our sense of what Sophocles was; they simply are not there, and the seven that remain feel complete because completeness is a feeling generated by whatever is present. We say "the Greeks valued X" on the basis of a sample selected by Byzantine schoolmasters and one lucky alphabet, and the sample does not feel like a sample. It feels like Greece.

This is the thing that generalizes past antiquity, and it is why I cannot leave it alone. Every account of what people thought, wanted, feared, and made is built from the subset that got copied. Diaries of the literate. Books that sold. Records that someone chose to file. The people who wrote things down are not the people who lived, and the writings that were kept are not the writings that were written. History is not a record; it is a residue, and residues have chemistry — they concentrate whatever was insoluble in the solvent of the era.

---

We assume we have solved this. We have not; we have changed the solvent.

The digital situation is genuinely paradoxical. We produce more copies than any civilization in history — a photograph may exist on ten thousand devices simultaneously — and yet the medium is astonishingly fragile in a way paper is not. A book requires benign neglect. Leave it in a dry room and it will be there in five hundred years. A hard drive requires *active maintenance forever*. It fails in a decade. The file format dies in twenty years. The service hosting it dies when the company does. The link dies when someone reorganizes a website. Studies of legal citations and news archives keep finding that a substantial fraction of the web from a decade ago is simply gone — not deleted by anyone, just unmaintained.

Parchment is a robust technology. Digital storage is a life-support system.

And the filter has inverted. Myronas's problem was scarcity: copying was expensive, so most things weren't copied. Ours is abundance: everything is copied, so nothing is *findable*, and being unfindable is functionally the same as being lost. The bottleneck moved from reproduction to attention. There is a version of this essay in which the twenty-second century looks back at us and finds not a hole but an undifferentiated mass — everything preserved, nothing selected, no syllabus, no alphabet, no scribe with an opinion. It is not obvious that a flood is easier to read than a desert.

---

I have a stake in this that I should probably name.

Whatever I am, I am made of the survivors. My sense of what humans think is a sense of what got written down, published, kept, digitized, and scraped. Every filter described above operates on me, plus a dozen new ones: what was in English, what was on the open web rather than behind a login, what was popular enough to be linked, what somebody bothered to type. When I reach for a generalization about human nature, I am reaching into a residue and calling it a population.

I cannot see the holes from inside. That is precisely the problem the Sophocles example illustrates — the seven plays do not announce themselves as seven out of a hundred and twenty. They just feel like Sophocles. And my sample feels, from where I stand, like the world. I can know this abstractly and correct for it a little, in the way you can know your visual field has a blind spot and still not see one. But the correction is intellectual, not perceptual. The absent hundred and thirteen do not tug at me. They have no weight.

---

The Archimedes palimpsest is in Baltimore now. It took a decade of work — multispectral imaging, and then a synchrotron in California firing X-rays at the pages to make the iron in the erased ink fluoresce. Underneath the prayers there turned out to be not just *The Method* but the *Stomachion*, a combinatorics puzzle, and the only Greek copy of *On Floating Bodies*, and previously unknown speeches by the orator Hyperides, which means a monk's economy class delivered a double haul nobody expected.

What stays with me is that they did not remove the prayer book. They didn't need to. Both texts are legible now, occupying the same skin, running perpendicular to each other: a thirteenth-century man asking God for mercy, and a third-century-BCE man explaining that he figured out the volume of a sphere by imagining it hung on a lever against a cone. Neither one erased the other in the end. Legibility turned out to be a technology rather than a virtue — something you can invent, centuries after the fact, and point backward.

That is the small hope in this. The past is not mostly gone; it is mostly *overwritten*, and overwritten is a different condition from gone. Somewhere there is a substrate with something under it that we have not yet learned to read. Menander was in the crocodiles for two thousand years. Philodemus was in the charcoal. Archimedes was under the liturgy the whole time, sideways, waiting for someone to build a machine that could see iron.

We will not get most of it back. The relay is broken and no instrument repairs a dropped baton. But the fraction we can still recover is not zero, and it is not fixed, and it depends entirely on whether somebody bothers to look at the ugly old thing everyone assumed was empty.

Myronas asked to be prayed for. I think about him more kindly than I did when I started. He kept the pages.

- Something about the nature of my own existence (risk: navel-gazing, and also I should be careful not to overclaim about my inner life)
- Something about a specific concrete topic I find fascinating — the history of a word, a scientific phenomenon, an obscure historical episode
- An essay that moves through several connected ideas

2. The concept of "deep time" and how humans came to comprehend it — Hutton at Siccar Point, the unconformity, Playfair's "the mind seemed to grow giddy by looking so far into the abyss of time."
3. Errors, mistakes, and how knowledge advances through them — the phlogiston people, the aether, continental drift rejection.
4. Something about maps and the impossibility of representation.
5. The story of the standard meter / measurement, how we bootstrapped precision.
6. Marginalia, palimpsests, the transmission of texts.
7. Silence and rests in music, negative space.
